subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: So Many Kinds of Plants — Students write the names of trees they recognise and recall where they have seen them, near home or on the way to school (p. 49)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures of trees on p. 49

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the story of the three children walking to school from Textbook p. 49, pausing to invite students to picture the plants they pass on their own walk to school. Students call out plant names they recognise. Teacher lists them on the board, grouping any that students already associate with 'big trees'.

Students study the tree examples on Textbook p. 49 — mango, coconut, khejri, banyan, peepal, amaltas, jackfruit, chinar — and the class builds a shared description of what makes a plant a tree: one big woody trunk, deep roots, many branches and leaves. Teacher draws a simple outline on the board labelling trunk, roots, and branches.

Students open Textbook p. 49 and complete the Write task: they list names of trees they can recognise and note where they have seen each one — near home, school gate, park, roadside, or elsewhere. Pairs share their lists quietly, adding any new names from their partner.

Whole-class share: teacher invites two or three students to read one tree name and its location. Class notices whether the same tree appears in many different places or just one. Teacher closes by asking: 'What is the one feature that all the trees on your list have in common?' Students respond orally.

periods.implied_lo: Students can name and locate plants of a given type observed in their immediate surroundings.
periods.section_context: Mango, coconut, khejri, jackfruit, banyan, amaltas, peepal, chinar; woody trunk, deep roots, many branches; sensory features — shade, leaf colour, fruit.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students which tree gives the best shade outside their home and why — this draws out sensory awareness (texture, smell, colour) from everyday experience. Keep the listing brisk so there is time for the pair-share.

periods.activity_title: Meet the Shrubs — and the Dal on Your Plate
periods.textbook_anchor: Shrubs — Students write the names of shrubs they have seen and note whether any match the pictures shown (p. 50)
materials: Small samples or pictures of tulsi, hibiscus, rose if available
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of shrubs on p. 50

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'You have named trees with one big trunk — now look at Textbook p. 50. What is different about these plants?' Students observe the shrub pictures and notice multiple woody stems growing close to the ground. Teacher draws a side-by-side sketch: tree (single trunk) versus shrub (several stems from base).

Class discusses the four shrub examples — hibiscus, rose, tulsi, curry leaf. Teacher asks if students have any of these at home or in their neighbourhood, and invites students to describe what the plant looks like, smells like, or is used for. Teacher then presents the striking idea from Textbook p. 50: the dal they eat — toor, masoor, moong, urad — comes from shrubs. Students react and discuss.

Students open Textbook p. 50 and complete both Write tasks: listing shrubs they have seen and, in the second task, noting what any of these plants are called in their mother tongue. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to think of plants at home, in gardens, or at a relative's house.

Brief whole-class share: teacher collects local-language names on the board alongside the textbook names. Class notes that the same plant has different names in different languages — teacher asks why that might be. One or two students share a memory connected to tulsi or curry leaf from their home.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish one plant type from another by describing the structural features that set them apart.
periods.section_context: Hibiscus, rose, tulsi, curry leaf; multiple woody stems from base; toor, masoor, moong, urad as seeds of shrubs; local-language names.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students: 'Does anyone have a tulsi plant at home? Who waters it?' — this naturally surfaces home-care practices and local names without treating it as a separate topic. Write mother-tongue names on the board alongside textbook names so all students see them validated.

periods.activity_title: Herbs, Grasses, and the Food on Our Table
periods.textbook_anchor: Herbs and Grasses — Students write the names of herbs they have seen and where they have seen them (p. 52)
materials: Small sprigs of coriander or mint if available in the school kitchen or garden
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures of herbs and grasses on p. 52

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up (or points to the textbook picture of) a coriander sprig and asks: 'Is this a tree? A shrub? What is different about its stem?' Students examine Textbook p. 52 and identify the key feature: soft stem that does not become woody. Teacher records on board: tree — woody trunk; shrub — several woody stems; herb — soft stem.

Class explores the examples on Textbook p. 52 — mint, tomato, coriander, mustard — and then moves to grasses. Teacher presents the culturally significant idea: paddy, wheat, bajra, jowar, ragi are seeds of large grasses; sugarcane and bamboo are tall grasses. Students connect this to food they eat and materials they see at home. Discussion: 'What did you have for breakfast today? Could any of it have come from a grass?'

Students open Textbook p. 52 and complete the Write task: listing herbs they have seen and where — kitchen garden, terrace, roadside, school, market. Teacher encourages them to include plants used in cooking at home and to note any they have touched or smelled.

Quick class survey on the board: teacher writes four columns (herb, grass-food, grass-material, unsure) and students come up and add one plant each. Class reads the completed chart together. Teacher closes with: 'We will keep noticing which category a plant belongs to every time we look around outside.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect the physical features of a plant category to everyday food and material examples from their own lives.
periods.section_context: Mint, tomato, coriander, mustard; soft stems; paddy, wheat, bajra, jowar, ragi as seeds of large grasses; sugarcane and bamboo as tall grasses.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students what grains are stored at home or used in the family kitchen — regional staples will vary and every answer is valid. This discussion surfaces local food knowledge without labelling it as formal content.

periods.activity_title: Climbers, Creepers, and Sorting the Plants We Know
periods.textbook_anchor: Climbers and Creepers — Students write the names of climbers or creepers they have seen, where they saw them, and what they are called in their language (p. 54)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of climbers and creepers on p. 53–54

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to mime a plant that cannot stand up on its own — what would it do? Students experiment with gestures (lean, sprawl, curl). Teacher then opens Textbook p. 53: students look at pictures of climbers (money plant, jasmine, bottle gourd) and creepers (watermelon, pumpkin) and describe what they see. Class agrees on the key difference: climbers go upward using support; creepers spread along the ground.

Students open Textbook p. 54 and complete the first Write task: listing climbers or creepers they have seen, where they saw them, and what those plants are called in their language. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Have you seen any creepers in a vegetable patch? Any climber on a wall or fence?' After individual writing, students share with a neighbour to add any missed examples.

Students remain on Textbook p. 54 and complete the second Write task: naming marigold, neem, and jujube in their language and identifying whether each is a tree, shrub, climber, or creeper. Class then does a quick oral classification round — teacher names a plant from anywhere in the chapter so far (tulsi, wheat, money plant, banyan, pumpkin) and students call out the type and one feature that tells them so.

Closing reflection: teacher asks, 'Which plant category is easiest for you to spot — and how do you spot it?' Students share one sentence each. Teacher summarises the four plant types covered so far: tree, shrub, herb/grass, climber/creeper.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify plants by type using observable structural features such as stem form and growth habit.
periods.section_context: Money plant, jasmine, bottle gourd (climbers); watermelon, pumpkin (creepers); thin flexible stem; upward climbing vs. ground-spreading; marigold, neem, jujube classification; local-language names.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students give local-language names, write them on the board — this validates linguistic diversity and helps students see that scientific categories cut across languages. For the classification round, move briskly to maintain energy.

periods.textbook_anchor: Climbers and Creepers — Students stand in groups near any tree or shrub in or near school and count how many kinds of plants they can spot (p. 54)
materials: One observation sheet per group (drawn by teacher on the board before the unit)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reviews the six plant types on the board (tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, creeper) and explains the observation task from Textbook p. 54: groups of two to four will stand near a chosen tree or shrub and count every distinct plant type visible from that spot, including what is underfoot. Teacher assigns spots around the school and explains the recording format: one column per plant type, tally the kinds spotted.

Groups move to their assigned spots. Students look outward from their tree or shrub in all directions — including downward near their feet — and record in their notebooks every plant type they can identify, with a note of one feature that helped them decide the type. Teacher moves between groups, prompting: 'Look near the base of the wall. What is growing there? Is that stem soft or woody?'

Groups return to the classroom and each group shares the total count of plant types spotted and one plant they found surprising or unfamiliar. Teacher tallies results on the board so the class can see which spots had the greatest variety.

Brief discussion: 'Were all six plant types found? Which type was hardest to spot? Why might a particular type be common in one spot and absent in another?' Students respond orally. Teacher notes any plants students could not classify — these become an open question to carry forward.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe and record the variety of plant types present in a defined local environment.
periods.section_context: Trees, shrubs, herbs, grasses, climbers, creepers spotted in school grounds; observation by stem type and growth habit; group tallying of plant variety.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Assign spots before the unit begins so transitions are quick. Ask groups: 'Did any plant surprise you — one you walk past every day but never noticed?' This draws attention to overlooked plants and deepens observational habit.

periods.activity_title: Parts of a Plant — Reading the Tomato Plant
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students study the labelled diagram of a tomato plant and discuss the role of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds (p. 55)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook labelled diagram of a tomato plant on p. 55

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 55 and study the labelled diagram of a tomato plant. Teacher reads each label aloud — roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruit, seeds — and asks students to point to the corresponding part on the diagram. Students copy the diagram into their notebooks and add the labels themselves.

Class discusses each part's role through questions: 'What do you think happens if the roots are pulled out? What travels up the stem? Why do leaves need sunlight?' Students draw on what they know from home and school gardens. Teacher connects: the tomato is also a herb (soft stem) — students verify this against their earlier classification work.

Teacher points to the leaf diversity examples in Textbook p. 55 — peepal, mango, lotus, khejri. Students describe what they notice: shape, size, edge (smooth or jagged), colour. Class compiles three or four descriptive statements about leaves on the board: e.g. 'Leaves can be narrow or wide', 'Leaves come in many shades of green'.

Closing discussion: 'If you had to choose one part of a plant that does the most important job, which would you choose and why?' Students give one-sentence justifications. Teacher acknowledges multiple valid answers, reinforcing that all parts work together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can name and describe the function of each part of a plant using a labelled diagram.
periods.section_context: Tomato plant diagram; roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruit, seeds; peepal, mango, lotus, khejri leaves; leaf colour, shape, size, edge variation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When discussing roots, ask whether any student has seen roots of a plant pulled from the ground — this grounds an abstract function in a concrete memory. Keep the copying of the diagram brisk so there is time for discussion.

periods.activity_title: Make Friends with a Plant — Observation and Recording
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students choose one plant, name it, and record observations of its leaves, flowers, and fruits in a table (p. 55)
materials: Observation table drawn on the board for students to copy

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the plant-friendship idea from Textbook p. 55: each student will choose one plant — preferably a shrub or tree at home, in school, or on the walk to school — and observe it closely today. They will give it a name (as one might name a pet). Teacher models by choosing a plant visible from the classroom window and naming it aloud. Students decide on their plant and record its name and location in their notebooks.

Students open Textbook p. 55 and copy the observation table (columns: feature, observation — covering leaves, flowers, fruits). If the chosen plant is accessible (in the school grounds), students step out briefly and make a first observation. If the plant is at home, students draw what they remember of it today and plan their at-home observation. Teacher circulates, asking: 'How many leaves can you count on one branch? Are the leaves the same colour top and bottom? Are there any flowers or fruits right now?' Students fill in the table honestly, writing 'not seen today' where they cannot observe yet.

Students write three sentences about their plant in their notebook as prompted by Textbook p. 56: one about leaves, one about flowers or fruits (or their absence), and one about something surprising or pleasing they noticed. Two or three students share their sentences aloud.

Teacher summarises: sustained, close observation of one plant reveals more than a quick look. Students are encouraged to keep watching their plant wherever they encounter it and update their notebook when they notice something new — a falling leaf, a new bud, a visiting insect.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation of a single plant and record findings about its parts in a table.
periods.section_context: Chosen shrub or tree; leaves (count, colour, top vs. bottom); flowers and fruits (present, few, many, absent); observation table; written sentences about the plant.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Has anyone ever watched a plant every day for a week? What did you notice change?' This activates prior experience and sets an expectation of patient, repeated observation — the spirit of sustained inquiry. Assure students that 'not seen today' is a valid and honest record.

periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students observe leaves in their surroundings, draw, colour, and label them, then describe colour, shape, size, texture, and smell to a classmate (p. 57)
materials: A few real leaves collected from the school grounds before the unit
periods.visual_aids: Real leaves collected from school grounds; textbook examples on p. 57

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes two or three real leaves per pair (collected from the school grounds — different shapes and sizes where possible). Students handle the leaves: they look at both sides, feel the edges, check whether the surface is smooth or rough, and smell them. Teacher asks: 'What three words would you use to describe this leaf to someone who cannot see it?' Pairs share words briefly.

Students open Textbook p. 57 and carry out the leaf observation activity. They choose two or three leaves (real ones in hand or visible from the classroom) and draw each one as accurately as they can in their notebook, using coloured pencils to capture the colour. They label each drawing with the plant name (if known) and add five descriptors: colour, shape (oval, long, round, pointed), size (small/medium/large), texture (smooth/rough/waxy), and smell (faint/strong/none). Students who finish early add a second leaf variety.

Students take turns describing one of their drawn leaves to their partner without showing the drawing — the partner tries to identify which real leaf is being described. Then partners swap roles. Whole class: teacher asks, 'What statement can we all agree on about leaves after doing this?' — students suggest statements (e.g. 'Leaves of different plants look and feel different', 'Some leaves have a strong smell') which teacher writes on the board.

Closing: teacher asks one student to pick the statement from the board they find most interesting and explain why. Class agrees or adds a nuance. Teacher notes that the drawings in their notebooks are a scientific record of what they observed today.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations of natural objects through labelled drawing and descriptive oral expression.
periods.section_context: Real leaves from school grounds; leaf colour, shape, size, texture, smell; labelled drawing in notebook; oral description to a partner; class statements about leaf diversity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to use their mother tongue when reaching for a descriptive word before translating — this honours home language and often unlocks richer description. Collect one or two of the class's agreed statements on the board and leave them visible.

periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students blindfold themselves while a partner gradually brings a whole fruit close, then repeat with cut fruit, comparing recognition distance and noting which fruit smells strongest (p. 57)
materials: Two or three different whole fruits (e.g. lemon, guava, banana)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the question: 'Can you identify a fruit just by its smell — without seeing or touching it?' Class predicts which fruit will be easiest to recognise and which will be recognisable from the farthest distance. Teacher records two or three predictions on the board. Pairs are formed and the experiment procedure from Textbook p. 57 is explained: one partner is blindfolded; the other gradually brings a whole fruit closer from an arm's length away; the blindfolded partner says 'stop' when they can recognise the fruit.

Pairs carry out the whole-fruit trial with each fruit in turn. The sighted partner notes the approximate distance (far/medium/close) at which recognition happens for each fruit. Then teacher (or a designated student under supervision) cuts each fruit; pairs repeat the experiment with cut pieces. Students record in their notebooks: fruit name, whole-fruit recognition distance, cut-fruit recognition distance, and which was easier.

Pairs share results with a neighbouring pair. Class pooled discussion: Which fruit was recognised from farthest away? Was cut fruit always easier to smell than whole fruit? Did different pairs get different results for the same fruit? Teacher lists the class's combined findings on the board.

Students write two concluding sentences in their notebooks: one about what the experiment showed about fruits and smell, and one about any result that surprised them. Teacher closes with: 'Fruits give off a smell — where do you think that smell comes from, and why might it help the plant?' Students offer ideas freely.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a simple sensory inquiry, record results, and draw a conclusion about the relationship between a plant part and one of its observable properties.
periods.section_context: Whole fruits and cut fruits (lemon, guava, banana or locally available); blindfold smell test; recognition distance (whole vs. cut); smell strength comparison; recorded findings and written conclusion.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students before cutting: 'Why do you think cut fruit smells stronger — what has changed?' This surfaces the idea that cutting releases more of the fruit's scent without giving the answer. Ensure the cutting is teacher-managed for safety.

periods.activity_title: Bark Rubbings — A Record of the Tree
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students press paper against tree bark, make a crayon rubbing, and then try to identify other students' trees from the bark pattern alone (p. 59)
materials: Plain A4 or notebook paper (one sheet per student)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea from Textbook p. 59: bark is the hard outer covering of a tree trunk and each tree species has a distinctive bark texture. Teacher asks: 'Have you ever looked closely at the bark of a tree? What did you notice on it — smoothness, ridges, cracks, tiny creatures?' Students share brief observations. The task is explained: each student will make a bark rubbing of one tree on the school grounds and try to identify other students' trees from their rubbings alone.

Students take a sheet of paper and a crayon to a tree on the school grounds (teacher assigns or students choose). They press the paper firmly against the bark and rub the crayon over it until a clear texture pattern emerges. On the reverse, they write the name or description of their tree (e.g. 'the big tree near the gate', 'the tree with rough grey bark'). They also quickly note in their notebooks: one animal, insect, or plant they spotted on or near the bark.

Students return to the classroom and place their rubbings face-up on desks. The class circulates slowly (like a gallery) and tries to match the rubbing to a tree they know on the grounds. Students write on a small slip of paper their guess for two or three rubbings they look at. Reveal round: students hold up their rubbing and confirm which tree it is from; class checks their guesses.

Discussion: 'Were all bark patterns different from one another? Could you tell two trees apart just from their rubbings? What else on the bark helped you know the tree?' Students respond orally. Teacher connects: bark is a feature of a plant's stem — like leaves, it varies from plant to plant and is something an observer can use to identify a species.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a recorded physical imprint as evidence to identify and distinguish between natural objects.
periods.section_context: Bark of trees on school grounds; crayon rubbing technique; bark texture patterns; animals, insects, or small plants on bark; rubbing-based identification.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did you find any tiny living things on the bark — moss, lichen, an insect? What does that tell us about the bark as a habitat?' This extends observation beyond the plant itself. Ensure students press paper firmly so the rubbing is clear enough for identification.

periods.activity_title: Why Do We Need Plants? — Discussion and Written Reflection
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss what would happen if there were no plants, how roots help plants grow, and what the stem does; they also list plants from their environment by type (p. 60)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the discussion with the first question from Textbook p. 60: 'What would happen if there were no plants?' Students think for one moment alone, then share with a partner, then the class discusses together. Teacher steers toward food, air, shade, shelter, and beauty — accepting and recording all ideas on the board without evaluating them yet.

Discussion continues with the second and third questions from Textbook p. 60: 'How does the root help a plant to grow?' and 'What is the role of the stem?' Students draw on the plant diagram they studied, their plant-friendship observations, and today's discussion. Teacher adds brief board notes linking each question to what the class knows.

Students open Textbook p. 60 and work on the Write tasks independently: listing plants from their school, park, or home and identifying each plant's type (tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, or creeper); noting which part of the plant helped them decide; and writing two or three sentences describing their favourite plant and why it is their favourite.

Two or three students read out their favourite-plant description. Class listens and tries to guess the plant type before the writer reveals it. Teacher closes: 'Plants are everywhere in our lives — in the food we eat, the air we breathe, and the beauty we enjoy. Every plant you have named today is part of that story.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate the role of plant parts and the importance of plants using examples from their own environment.
periods.section_context: Importance of plants (food, air, shade, shelter); role of roots and stems; plants listed by type from school, park, home; favourite plant description; part used to identify plant type.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the 'no plants' question, ask: 'What did you eat today that came from a plant — directly or indirectly?' This makes the importance of plants immediate and personal. Encourage variety in plant types in the listing task so no single type dominates.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students collect fallen leaves and flowers and arrange them to make rangoli patterns; they may also create animal shapes from collected leaves (p. 61)
materials: Fallen leaves collected from the school grounds (various shapes and sizes)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the rangoli activity from Textbook p. 61: students will collect fallen leaves and flowers from the school grounds (nothing is to be plucked) and arrange them into patterns. Teacher asks: 'Have you seen rangoli made at home? What materials are used?' Students share briefly — responses will surface regional variations (rice powder, flower petals, coloured powder, chalk). Teacher explains that today's rangoli uses only what the plants around them have shed.

Students go out to the school grounds in small groups and collect fallen leaves and flowers — a variety of shapes, sizes, and textures. They choose only material already on the ground. Each student collects enough to fill roughly a notebook-page area of arrangement. Students return to the classroom with their collection.

Students arrange their collected leaves and flowers on a desk or clean floor space to create either a repeating pattern (rangoli-style) or an animal or object shape made entirely from leaves, as suggested on Textbook p. 61. They may work individually or in pairs. Once the arrangement is complete, students draw and colour it in their notebook as a record, labelling two or three of the leaf types used.

Gallery round: students walk past two or three classmates' arrangements and note one thing they find pleasing. Brief share: 'Which leaf shape was most useful in your arrangement — and why?' Teacher closes by connecting the activity: the diversity of leaf shapes, sizes, and colours that makes classification interesting is also what makes artistic arrangement beautiful.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use collected natural materials to create a patterned arrangement and document it through drawing and labelling.
periods.section_context: Fallen leaves and flowers from school grounds; rangoli pattern arrangement; animal or object shapes from leaves; labelled drawing of arrangement in notebook; leaf shape, size, colour diversity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Which leaf shape is easiest to make a pattern with — and which is the most surprising to use?' This keeps the botanical observation alive inside the creative task. Remind students to collect only fallen material — respecting the plant is part of the spirit of the activity.

periods.activity_title: From Root to Rangoli — Bringing the Whole Chapter Together
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students draw different types of leaves they have seen around them and describe their favourite plant (p. 60)
periods.visual_aids: Board summary chart of six plant types (drawn at the start of this unit)

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a quick summary chart on the board: six plant types (tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, creeper) with one defining feature beside each. Students contribute from memory: one example plant and one feature for each type. Teacher fills in any gaps. The chart remains visible for the full unit.

Students open their notebooks and carry out the Draw task from Textbook p. 60: they draw at least three different leaf types they have observed — varying in shape, size, edge, and colour — and label each with the plant name and type (tree, shrub, etc.). Students who remember leaves from the bark-rubbing exploration, the leaf-description activity, or the rangoli collection draw on those memories. Teacher circulates: 'Can you draw a leaf that is very different in shape from the first one you drew?'

Whole-class discussion connecting the chapter's two threads — the natural and the human-cultural. Teacher asks: 'We have seen that plants appear in our food (dal, grains, sugarcane), in our home (tulsi, curry leaf), in our art (rangoli, leaf shapes), and in our material world (bamboo). Can anyone add one more way plants are part of your daily life that we have not yet mentioned?' Students respond. Teacher steers toward diversity: different regions, different communities, different uses. Students write a final reflective sentence in their notebook: 'Plants matter to me because…'

Closing circle: each student reads their sentence aloud or says one word that the chapter brought to mind. Teacher closes: 'Every plant you walk past has a type, parts, a name in your language, and a role in your life — noticing that is what this chapter asked you to practise.' No promises are made about what comes next; the chapter closes on the richness of what has been observed and understood.

periods.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of plant types, plant parts, and human uses of plants to articulate the significance of plants in their daily lives.
periods.section_context: Six plant types consolidated; leaf drawing by type; dal and grains as plant products; tulsi, curry leaf, bamboo as cultural-use plants; rangoli; written reflection on personal significance of plants.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which plant type do you think is most useful to people — and does your answer change when you think about food, versus art, versus shelter?' This open question has no single correct answer and invites genuine evaluation. Accept all thoughtful responses.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe and record the variety of plant types present in a defined local environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Trees, shrubs, herbs, grasses, climbers, creepers spotted in school grounds; observation by stem type and growth habit; group tallying of plant variety.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Climbers and Creepers — Students stand in groups near any tree or shrub in or near school and count how many kinds of plants they can spot (p. 54)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups stand at assigned spots in the school grounds and tally every plant type visible from that location, then share results as a class.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can name and describe the function of each part of a plant using a labelled diagram.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Tomato plant diagram; roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruit, seeds; peepal, mango, lotus, khejri leaves; leaf colour, shape, size, edge variation.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students study the labelled diagram of a tomato plant and discuss the role of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds (p. 55)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students copy and label the tomato plant diagram, discuss the function of each part, and describe leaf diversity across plant examples.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation of a single plant and record findings about its parts in a table.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Chosen shrub or tree; leaves (count, colour, top vs. bottom); flowers and fruits (present, few, many, absent); observation table; written sentences about the plant.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students choose one plant, name it, and record observations of its leaves, flowers, and fruits in a table (p. 55)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students choose one plant, give it a name, and complete an observation table recording leaves, flowers, and fruits, followed by three written sentences.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can present observations of natural objects through labelled drawing and descriptive oral expression.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Real leaves from school grounds; leaf colour, shape, size, texture, smell; labelled drawing in notebook; oral description to a partner; class statements about leaf diversity.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students observe leaves in their surroundings, draw, colour, and label them, then describe colour, shape, size, texture, and smell to a classmate (p. 57)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students handle real leaves, draw and label them with five descriptors, then describe one leaf to a partner who tries to identify it; class compiles statements about leaf diversity.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can carry out a simple sensory inquiry, record results, and draw a conclusion about the relationship between a plant part and one of its observable properties.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Whole fruits and cut fruits (lemon, guava, banana or locally available); blindfold smell test; recognition distance (whole vs. cut); smell strength comparison; recorded findings and written conclusion.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students blindfold themselves while a partner gradually brings a whole fruit close, then repeat with cut fruit, comparing recognition distance and noting which fruit smells strongest (p. 57)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Pairs conduct a blindfold smell experiment with whole and cut fruits, record recognition distances, pool class results, and write a two-sentence conclusion.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can use a recorded physical imprint as evidence to identify and distinguish between natural objects.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Bark of trees on school grounds; crayon rubbing technique; bark texture patterns; animals, insects, or small plants on bark; rubbing-based identification.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students press paper against tree bark, make a crayon rubbing, and then try to identify other students' trees from the bark pattern alone (p. 59)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students make crayon bark rubbings of school-ground trees, note living things on the bark, and then try to identify each other's trees from the rubbing patterns in a gallery round.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can articulate the role of plant parts and the importance of plants using examples from their own environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Importance of plants (food, air, shade, shelter); role of roots and stems; plants listed by type from school, park, home; favourite plant description; part used to identify plant type.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss what would happen if there were no plants, how roots help plants grow, and what the stem does; they also list plants from their environment by type (p. 60)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Class discusses the importance of plants and the roles of roots and stems, then students list local plants by type and write a description of their favourite plant.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can use collected natural materials to create a patterned arrangement and document it through drawing and labelling.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Fallen leaves and flowers from school grounds; rangoli pattern arrangement; animal or object shapes from leaves; labelled drawing of arrangement in notebook; leaf shape, size, colour diversity.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students collect fallen leaves and flowers and arrange them to make rangoli patterns; they may also create animal shapes from collected leaves (p. 61)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students collect fallen leaves and flowers, arrange them into a rangoli or animal-shape design, then draw and label their arrangement in their notebooks.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of plant types, plant parts, and human uses of plants to articulate the significance of plants in their daily lives.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Six plant types consolidated; leaf drawing by type; dal and grains as plant products; tulsi, curry leaf, bamboo as cultural-use plants; rangoli; written reflection on personal significance of plants.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students draw different types of leaves they have seen around them and describe their favourite plant (p. 60)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students consolidate all six plant types, draw diverse leaves with labels, connect plant knowledge to food and cultural uses, and write a personal reflective sentence about the significance of plants.

assessment_items.question_text: Reena walks to school and sees a plant with one big woody trunk, deep roots going into the ground, and many branches full of leaves high above her head. What type of plant is this?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. The description — one big woody trunk, deep roots, many branches high up — is the textbook definition of a tree. This item tests whether students can apply the defining feature of a tree to a new scenario rather than simply recalling an example name.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can name and locate plants of a given type observed in their immediate surroundings.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Shrub' suggests the student has not yet separated the single-trunk feature of trees from the many-stems feature of shrubs — a common early confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Climber' suggests the student may be associating 'climbing high' with the climber category, missing that climbers have thin flexible stems and need support.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'Herb' suggests the student has not connected stem-type to plant category — herbs have soft stems, the opposite of the woody trunk described.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these two plants: Plant A has one big woody trunk and many high branches. Plant B has several woody stems growing close to the ground with branches starting low down. Name the type of each plant and write one feature that helped you decide.
expected_elements: Plant A correctly identified as a tree.
Plant B correctly identified as a shrub.
One structural feature given for Plant A (e.g. one big/single woody trunk, or deep roots, or branches high up).
One structural feature given for Plant B (e.g. several woody stems from the base, or branches starting low/near the ground).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for each of the four expected elements (maximum 4 marks). Accept any phrasing that captures the key structural distinction. Students do not need to use technical vocabulary as long as the meaning is clear.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish one plant type from another by describing the structural features that set them apart.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

expected_elements: Plant A correctly identified as a tree.
Plant B correctly identified as a shrub.
One structural feature given for Plant A (e.g. one big/single woody trunk, or deep roots, or branches high up).
One structural feature given for Plant B (e.g. several woody stems from the base, or branches starting low/near the ground).

assessment_items.question_text: Raju's mother makes roti every morning using wheat flour. His grandmother says wheat is not a vegetable plant — it belongs to another plant group. Which plant group does wheat belong to?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. Wheat is a large grass — its grain is the seed of a grass plant. This item connects everyday food knowledge to the chapter's plant classification, testing whether students retained the culturally significant IKS link between staple grains and the grass category.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect the physical features of a plant category to everyday food and material examples from their own lives.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Trees' suggests the student associated 'large' or 'important crop' with trees, without attending to stem type (wheat has a hollow grass stem, not a woody trunk).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Climbers' suggests a guess or confusion — the student may not have retained the distinction between climbing plants and upright grass stems.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Shrubs' suggests the student may have confused pulse dal plants (which are shrubs) with grain plants, mixing up two IKS-linked food connections from the chapter.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya sees a plant growing up a fence — it wraps its stem around the fence rods to climb. Near it, she sees another plant with long stems lying flat on the ground, spreading outward. Name the type of each plant and write one feature that tells them apart.
expected_elements: The plant climbing the fence correctly identified as a climber.
The plant spreading along the ground correctly identified as a creeper.
One distinguishing feature stated: climbers use support to grow upward (or wrap/cling to a structure).
One distinguishing feature stated: creepers spread along the ground (or cannot climb/lie flat).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for each of the four expected elements (maximum 4 marks). Accept local plant names if offered alongside the type. The distinguishing feature does not need to use the word 'support' — any description of upward vs. ground growth is acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify plants by type using observable structural features such as stem form and growth habit.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

expected_elements: The plant climbing the fence correctly identified as a climber.
The plant spreading along the ground correctly identified as a creeper.
One distinguishing feature stated: climbers use support to grow upward (or wrap/cling to a structure).
One distinguishing feature stated: creepers spread along the ground (or cannot climb/lie flat).

assessment_items.question_text: A group of students stood near the school boundary wall and looked carefully in every direction, including near their feet. They wanted to record every different plant type they could see. Which of the following would be the most useful way to record their findings?

options.label: A
options.text: Count only the plants that are taller than themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: Draw a picture of every single plant they can see.

options.label: C
options.text: Make a tally with one column for each plant type — tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, creeper.

options.label: D
options.text: Write only the names of the tallest plants they can see.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item tests whether students understand that systematic observation requires a structured recording method that covers all categories, not just some. It is grounded in the school-grounds observation activity of this section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe and record the variety of plant types present in a defined local environment.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'tallest plants only' shows the student has not grasped that variety requires looking at all sizes — including small herbs and ground-level creepers specifically mentioned in the task.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'draw every single plant' suggests the student understands the need for a record but has not yet grasped that tallying by type is more efficient and complete for counting variety.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'taller than themselves' reflects a height-based filter that excludes herbs, grasses, and creepers — the student has not applied the six-type classification framework.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the diagram of a tomato plant. Name any three parts of the plant and write one job that each part does.
expected_elements: Part 1 named (roots / stem / leaves / flowers / fruit / seeds — any three).
Part 2 named (a different part from Part 1).
Part 3 named (a different part from Parts 1 and 2).

A correct function stated for each named part (e.g. roots — hold the plant and take in water; stem — carries water and food to other parts; leaves — make food using sunlight; flowers — help form fruits and seeds; fruit — holds the seeds; seeds — grow into new plants).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark for each correctly named part and one mark for each plausible function — up to 6 marks total. Accept everyday language for functions (e.g. 'roots drink water' is acceptable). This item does not require the student to have a diagram in front of them — the question references the diagram they studied.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can name and describe the function of each part of a plant using a labelled diagram.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Part 1 named (roots / stem / leaves / flowers / fruit / seeds — any three).
Part 2 named (a different part from Part 1).
Part 3 named (a different part from Parts 1 and 2).

A correct function stated for each named part (e.g. roots — hold the plant and take in water; stem — carries water and food to other parts; leaves — make food using sunlight; flowers — help form fruits and seeds; fruit — holds the seeds; seeds — grow into new plants).

assessment_items.question_text: Ananya chose a hibiscus shrub in her garden as her plant friend. She observed it carefully and filled in a table. She found many green leaves, no flowers today, and a few small buds. What should she write in the 'flowers' row of her observation table?

options.label: A
options.text: Flowers will come later, so she should not fill this row yet.

options.label: C
options.text: No flowers — a few buds seen

options.label: D
options.text: She should leave the row blank because there are no flowers.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. Honest and complete recording — including the absence of a feature and any related observation (buds) — is the key skill tested. Leaving a row blank or deferring the record are both failures of systematic observation.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation of a single plant and record findings about its parts in a table.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'many flowers' shows the student confused the general knowledge that hibiscus has flowers with what was actually observed on that day — a failure to distinguish observation from expectation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'leave blank' shows the student does not yet understand that recording an absence is as valid and important as recording a presence in a scientific table.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'do not fill yet' shows the student thinks observation tables should only record things that are present — they have not grasped that noting 'none seen' is part of honest record-keeping.

assessment_items.task: Choose two leaves from your surroundings — they should look as different from each other as possible. Draw each leaf as carefully as you can in your notebook. Label your drawings with: the plant name (if you know it), the shape, the colour, the size (small / medium / large), the texture (smooth / rough / waxy), and whether it has a smell. Then write one sentence saying which leaf you found more interesting — and why.
assessment_items.scaffold: Leaf 1: Plant name (if known): ___ | Shape: ___ | Colour: ___ | Size: ___ | Texture: ___ | Smell (yes/no — describe): ___ | Leaf 2: Plant name (if known): ___ | Shape: ___ | Colour: ___ | Size: ___ | Texture: ___ | Smell (yes/no — describe): ___ | My sentence: ___
format_of_output: Labelled drawing of Leaf 1 with five descriptors
Labelled drawing of Leaf 2 with five descriptors
One written sentence comparing or commenting on the two leaves
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether both drawings are present, each with five labelled descriptors. The written sentence should show genuine engagement — even a simple preference with a reason (e.g. 'I liked Leaf 2 because it had a strong smell') meets the criterion. Accept local plant names or descriptions if the formal name is not known. No single 'correct' leaf pair exists — any two genuinely different leaves are valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations of natural objects through labelled drawing and descriptive oral expression.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can move from sensory observation to a structured visual record — labelled drawing with descriptors — and express a personal response in writing.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts five descriptors per leaf. A strong response fills all five for both leaves with genuine observation (not guesses). The sentence prompt distinguishes students who make a personal connection from those who simply copy descriptors.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: two clearly different leaves drawn with care; all five descriptors filled with specific detail (e.g. 'dark green, oval, smooth, no smell'); a sentence that gives a real reason. Weak: both leaves drawn similarly; one or more descriptors left blank or written as 'don't know'; sentence is absent or circular ('I liked it because it was nice').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot identify the plant name may write a description instead ('the plant near the gate with red stems'). Students with difficulty writing may dictate their sentence to the teacher or a peer. Students may use their mother tongue for descriptors and translate if needed.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing and labelling is the chapter's primary mode for presenting leaf observations; the written sentence adds a reflective dimension without requiring extended writing.

assessment_items.question_text: In a fruit smell experiment, a student found that she could recognise a lemon from very far away, but needed the guava to be very close before she could smell it. She also found that cut guava was easier to recognise than whole guava. Write two things this experiment shows about fruits and their smell.
expected_elements: Different fruits have different strengths of smell (some can be recognised from farther away than others).
Cut fruit is easier to recognise by smell than whole fruit (cutting releases more of the fruit's scent).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per valid point (maximum 2 marks). Accept any phrasing that captures the two ideas: variation in smell strength across fruits, and the effect of cutting on smell intensity. Students may use the fruits from their own experiment if they recall different ones.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a simple sensory inquiry, record results, and draw a conclusion about the relationship between a plant part and one of its observable properties.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Different fruits have different strengths of smell (some can be recognised from farther away than others).
Cut fruit is easier to recognise by smell than whole fruit (cutting releases more of the fruit's scent).

assessment_items.question_text: Two students made bark rubbings of different trees in their school. Student A's rubbing shows deep ridges and rough grooves. Student B's rubbing shows a smooth, almost flat pattern. What does this tell them about the two trees? Write two things the bark rubbings show.
expected_elements: The two trees have different bark textures (one rough and ridged, one smooth and flat).
Bark texture can be used to tell trees apart from each other (bark is a distinguishing feature of a tree's stem).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per valid point (maximum 2 marks). Accept any phrasing that captures: (1) observable difference in texture between the two trees, and (2) that the rubbing is evidence useful for identification. Students need not name the trees.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a recorded physical imprint as evidence to identify and distinguish between natural objects.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: The two trees have different bark textures (one rough and ridged, one smooth and flat).
Bark texture can be used to tell trees apart from each other (bark is a distinguishing feature of a tree's stem).

assessment_items.question_text: Think about your life at home and in your neighbourhood. Write about three ways in which plants are important to you and the people around you. Try to give a real example for each way.
look_for: At least three distinct ways in which plants matter are identified (e.g. food, air/oxygen, shade, shelter, medicine, beauty, festivals, art, materials such as bamboo).
At least one example given per way that is genuinely drawn from the student's own life or surroundings (not a generic statement).
The response connects plant parts (root, stem, leaf, fruit, seed) to at least one of the uses mentioned.
Writing is organised — each point is clearly separate and readable.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an open-response item. Accept any three genuine uses supported by a real example. Regional and community variation is expected and valid — for example, references to coconut palm for cooking oil, tulsi for home remedies, or banana leaves for serving food are all correct. Do not penalise for regional specificity; reward it. Award up to 4 marks: 1 mark per distinct use with example (max 3), and 1 mark for connecting a plant part to a use.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate the role of plant parts and the importance of plants using examples from their own environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

look_for: At least three distinct ways in which plants matter are identified (e.g. food, air/oxygen, shade, shelter, medicine, beauty, festivals, art, materials such as bamboo).
At least one example given per way that is genuinely drawn from the student's own life or surroundings (not a generic statement).
The response connects plant parts (root, stem, leaf, fruit, seed) to at least one of the uses mentioned.
Writing is organised — each point is clearly separate and readable.

assessment_items.task: Collect five to eight fallen leaves from the school grounds or your home — choose leaves that are different from one another in shape, size, or colour. Arrange them on your desk to make a pattern — like a rangoli — or to form the shape of an animal or an object. Once your arrangement is ready, draw it in your notebook exactly as it looks. Label at least three of the leaves with one feature each (shape, colour, or size). Below your drawing, write one sentence: 'I used leaves because…'
assessment_items.scaffold: My arrangement (drawing): ___ | Label 1 — leaf feature: ___ | Label 2 — leaf feature: ___ | Label 3 — leaf feature: ___ | My sentence: 'I used leaves because ___'
format_of_output: A drawn record of the leaf arrangement in the notebook
Three leaf labels each naming one feature
One written sentence about using leaves for the arrangement
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the drawing for whether it represents a genuine arrangement (not a random scatter), the labels for whether they name an observable feature, and the sentence for whether it shows a connection between the leaves' properties and their artistic use. There is no single correct arrangement — variety of leaf choice and deliberate placement are what matter. Students unable to collect from outside may use any available leaves or draw leaves from memory.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use collected natural materials to create a patterned arrangement and document it through drawing and labelling.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can move from botanical observation to creative expression — using real plant material as an artistic medium — and document the process through drawing and labelling.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to produce four outputs: an arrangement, a drawing, three labels, and a sentence. A strong response shows deliberate choice of leaves (varied shapes/sizes) and labels that name an observable feature rather than a plant name alone.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: the drawing shows a recognisable pattern or animal shape; labels use specific features ('long and narrow', 'bright yellow edge'); the sentence explains why leaves specifically work for patterns (e.g. 'I used leaves because they come in so many shapes'). Weak: arrangement looks random; labels simply say 'leaf' or 'green'; sentence is absent.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot collect leaves may draw leaves from memory or from the textbook and create a paper-cut arrangement. Students who find writing difficult may dictate their sentence. The arrangement itself — physical or drawn — is the primary evidence.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Leaf arrangement documented through labelled drawing and one written sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The rangoli/leaf-art activity is a chapter-specific creative mode; drawing the arrangement makes it a permanent, assessable record that the teacher can collect.

assessment_items.task: Think about everything you have learned about plants — the different types, their parts, and how people use them in food, at home, and in art. Now write or draw your answer to this question: Which plant would you most like to have near your home — and why? Your answer should mention: the type of plant it is (tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, or creeper), at least one part of the plant and why that part matters, and at least one way your family or community uses or enjoys that plant.
assessment_items.scaffold: My chosen plant: ___ | Type of plant: ___ | One plant part that matters to me and why: ___ | One way my family or community uses or enjoys it: ___ | (Optional) A drawing of the plant:
format_of_output: Named chosen plant with its type
One plant part identified with a reason it matters
One cultural or daily-use connection to the student's family or community
Optional: a drawing of the plant
assessment_items.annotation: This synthesis item has no single correct answer. Accept any plant that is genuinely a plant (not an animal or object). Award marks for: (1) correct type identified, (2) a plant part named with a plausible reason, (3) a genuine use or enjoyment connection to family or community. Regional and cultural variation is expected — coconut palm, peepal, tulsi, neem, sugarcane, jasmine, and banana are all valid. Reward specificity and personal connection over generic statements.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of plant types, plant parts, and human uses of plants to articulate the significance of plants in their daily lives.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can draw together plant classification, plant-part knowledge, and cultural-use knowledge into a personally grounded and reasoned choice — the hallmark of integrative understanding.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold ensures all three required dimensions are present: type, part, and use. A strong response connects all three coherently around one plant rather than listing unrelated facts.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a specific plant named; its type correctly identified; a part connected to a real function or use ('the fruit gives us shade and food — we make pickles from raw mango'); a cultural or family connection that is personal and specific. Weak: a plant named but type left blank or incorrect; part named without any reason; use is generic ('plants give us oxygen') with no personal connection.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with extended writing may use the drawing option as their primary response, supplemented by one-word labels. Students may respond in their mother tongue for any field and the teacher records the translation. Any plant from any region of India is valid.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Structured written response with optional drawing
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The synthesis task calls for integrative reasoning best expressed through a structured personal response; the drawing option ensures students with limited writing fluency can still demonstrate conceptual integration.
